boina.t: The northern Sakalava kingdom of Madagascar, whose port of Mahajanga became a thriving hub of Indian Ocean trade in the 18th century.
boina.o: Boina was founded around 1690 by Andriamandisoarivo, a prince of the Maroserana dynasty of Menabe, who led followers north and conquered the north-west coast. The kingdom took over the trading towns of the Antalaotra, Swahili-speaking Muslim merchants, and later centred on Majunga (Mahajanga).
boina.r: Sakalava kingship rested on sacred royal relics and ancestor cults, while Muslim and Indian merchants ran the port trade in slaves, cattle and rice with Arabia, the Swahili coast and the Comoros. Boina reached its height under Queen Ravahiny in the late 18th century, when Mahajanga was one of the busiest ports in the western Indian Ocean.
boina.e: The Merina Kingdom under Radama I captured Mahajanga in 1824. King Andriantsoly fled and later took over the Sultanate of Mayotte, and Sakalava resistance in Boina collapsed by around 1840. Royal relic rituals still take place at Mahajanga.
boina.re: Traditional Malagasy religion, Islam among merchants

bar-kokhba-state.t: The short-lived Jewish state of Simon bar Kosiba, whose revolt against Hadrian was the last great Jewish rising against Rome.
bar-kokhba-state.o: The revolt broke out in 132, probably provoked by Hadrian's plan to refound Jerusalem as the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina, and possibly by a ban on circumcision. Its leader, Simon bar Kosiba, was hailed as Bar Kokhba, 'son of the star', a messianic title reportedly endorsed by Rabbi Akiva.
bar-kokhba-state.r: Simon styled himself Nasi (prince) of Israel and dated documents by the 'redemption of Israel'. Coins overstruck on Roman issues showed the Temple facade and the slogan 'for the freedom of Jerusalem'. Letters and contracts found in caves of the Judaean Desert, notably Nahal Hever, show a working administration that leased state land, collected produce and gave terse orders to commanders, written in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek.
bar-kokhba-state.e: Hadrian brought in Julius Severus from Britain, who wore the rebels down with a war of sieges. The fortress of Betar fell in 135 or 136. Judea was devastated, renamed Syria Palaestina, and Jews were barred from Jerusalem.

beylik-of-mani.t: Semi-autonomous Ottoman principality of the Mani peninsula, whose last bey, Petrobey Mavromichalis, helped launch the Greek War of Independence.
beylik-of-mani.o: The Maniots of the southern Peloponnese had always resisted Ottoman control. After the failed Orlov revolt of 1770 and the Russo-Turkish peace of 1774, the Ottomans gave up direct rule and in 1776 created a Beylik of Mani under the authority of the Kapudan Pasha, the Ottoman admiral, with a Maniot bey.
beylik-of-mani.r: The bey, chosen from the Maniot clans, paid a modest tribute and kept order, but power remained with the feuding chieftain families in their stone tower houses. Notable beys included Tzanetos Grigorakis and, from 1815, Petros Mavromichalis. The Mani was poor, with olive oil, piracy and a strong warrior tradition shaping its society.
beylik-of-mani.e: In March 1821 Petrobey Mavromichalis declared revolt at Areopolis and Kalamata, joining the Greek War of Independence. The beylik ended, and the Mani became part of the First Hellenic Republic, though its clans long resisted central government.

barca.t: A Greek city of Cyrenaica founded by rebel Battiad princes, remembered for its brutal destruction by the Persians.
barca.o: Herodotus relates that around 560 BCE the brothers of King Arcesilaus II of the Kingdom of Cyrene quarrelled with him and founded Barca, on the plain inland from the coast (near modern al-Marj), with the support of local Libyans. The city soon became a rival of its mother city.
barca.r: Barca was a Greek city of mixed Greek and Libyan population, ruled at first by kings; Herodotus names a king Alazeir, whose daughter married Arcesilaus III of Cyrene. It was known for horse breeding and chariots. When Arcesilaus III was murdered there, his mother Pheretime called in the Persian governor of Egypt, Aryandes, whose army took Barca around 515 BCE by trickery after a long siege.
barca.e: Many Barcaeans were deported to Bactria. The city recovered as a member of the Cyrenaican cities, but declined as its port, Ptolemais, grew. It passed to the Ptolemaic Empire in 322 BCE.

batlokwa-chiefdom.t: The Sotho-speaking Tlokwa chiefdom led by the regent MaNthatisi and her son Sekonyela, a major power and raider during the wars of the 1820s.
batlokwa-chiefdom.o: The Tlokwa were a Sotho-speaking people of the upper Wilge and Caledon river region. When Hlubi and Ngwane refugees broke into the highveld in the early 1820s, the regent MaNthatisi led the Tlokwa on a long series of migrations and raids that made her name feared across the interior, before they settled around the mountain fortresses of Joalaboholo and Marabeng near modern Ficksburg.
batlokwa-chiefdom.r: Power rested on cattle, mountain strongholds and fighting men drawn from many uprooted groups. MaNthatisi handed authority to her son Sekonyela, whose rivalry with Moshoeshoe of the Basotho Kingdom dominated the Caledon valley for two decades. Sekonyela received Wesleyan missionaries but kept to traditional religion, and he clashed in turn with the Voortrekkers, who made him return stolen horses and cattle in 1837.
batlokwa-chiefdom.e: In 1853 Moshoeshoe stormed the Tlokwa strongholds and Sekonyela fled; he died in the Orange Free State. Most of his people were absorbed into the Basotho, while others later settled at Witsieshoek in the Free State, where a Tlokwa chieftaincy survives.

batawana-chiefdom.t: A Tswana chiefdom of Ngamiland around the Okavango delta, founded by a breakaway branch of the Bangwato.
batawana-chiefdom.o: Around 1795 Tawana, a son of the Bangwato chief, broke away after a succession dispute and led his followers north-west. They eventually settled near Lake Ngami at the edge of the Okavango delta, where they established authority over the BaYei, Hambukushu and other local peoples.
batawana-chiefdom.r: Batawana chiefs ruled from towns near Lake Ngami, drawing tribute in labour and goods from subject peoples. Ngamiland was rich in ivory and ostrich feathers, and the chiefdom traded with Cape and Griqua hunters and merchants. David Livingstone reached Lake Ngami in 1849 during the reign of Letsholathebe I.
batawana-chiefdom.e: Ngamiland was brought into the Bechuanaland Protectorate in the 1880s and 1890s, and the chiefdom continued under colonial rule. Maun became the capital and grew into the main town of north-western Botswana.

billung-march.t: A Saxon frontier march facing the Obotrites along the lower Elbe, held by the Billung family until the great Slavic revolt of 1066.
billung-march.o: Around 936 Otto I entrusted Hermann Billung with command against the Slavs along the lower Elbe, from Holstein to the Peene. This frontier region, later called the Billung March, covered roughly modern Mecklenburg and eastern Holstein, inhabited mainly by Obotrites and other Wendish peoples who paid tribute.
billung-march.r: The march was less a settled territory than a zone of military overlordship and tribute collection. The Billungs, who also became dukes of Saxony, controlled it from strongholds along the Elbe. Bishoprics such as Oldenburg in Holstein were founded to convert the Slavs, but German control remained loose and the Obotrite princes kept considerable power.
billung-march.e: The Great Slav Rising of 983 shook German control, and after the murder of the Christian Obotrite prince Gottschalk in 1066 the Slavs expelled German influence and destroyed churches. The march ceased to exist; German rule returned only with Henry the Lion in the 12th century, leading to the Lordship of Mecklenburg.

banu-ghaniya-majorca.t: The last Almoravid state, ruled from Majorca by the Banu Ghaniya, who waged a long war against the Almohads from the Balearics to Ifriqiya.
banu-ghaniya-majorca.o: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Ghaniya, of an Almoravid family related to the ruling dynasty, governed the Balearic Islands from about 1126. When the Almoravid Empire collapsed in the 1140s, he kept the islands as an independent emirate loyal to the Abbasid caliph.
banu-ghaniya-majorca.r: Under Ishaq ibn Muhammad (c. 1155-1183) Majorca prospered on trade and corsair raids, and made treaties with Genoa and Pisa. In 1184 Ali ibn Ghaniya invaded North Africa, seizing Bejaia and starting a war against the Almohads in Ifriqiya that lasted half a century.
banu-ghaniya-majorca.e: The Almohads conquered Majorca in 1203, killing its ruler Abd Allah ibn Ishaq, though the family fought on in Ifriqiya. James I of Aragon took Majorca in 1229, later forming the Kingdom of Majorca.

banu-khalid-emirate.t: The Bedouin emirate that ruled eastern Arabia from Hofuf after expelling the Ottomans, until the first Saudi state absorbed it.
banu-khalid-emirate.o: The Banu Khalid were a powerful tribal confederation of eastern Arabia. In 1670 their chief Barrak ibn Ghurayr expelled the Ottoman garrison of the Lahsa Eyalet and made Hofuf the centre of an emirate controlling the coast from Kuwait to Qatar and the oases of al-Hasa and Qatif.
banu-khalid-emirate.r: The emirs governed through tribal alliances, taxing oasis farmers, pearl divers and caravans while keeping nominal ties with the Ottoman Empire. Under their protection, clans of the Bani Utbah settled at Kuwait and later Zubarah in Qatar. Sulayman ibn Muhammad, emir in the mid-18th century, pressured the town of Uyayna to expel the reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab.
banu-khalid-emirate.e: Family feuds after 1752 weakened the emirate. The Emirate of Diriyah defeated the Banu Khalid in a series of campaigns and conquered al-Hasa by 1796, though the tribe remained important in the region.

balearica.t: The late Roman province of the Balearic Islands, separated from Carthaginiensis in the 4th century and lost to the Vandals in 455.
balearica.o: The Balearic Islands, conquered by Rome in 123 BCE, belonged to Hispania Citerior, Tarraconensis and then Carthaginiensis. Around 369 they became a separate province, Balearica, under a governor in the Diocese of Hispania.
balearica.r: The islands lived from farming, fishing and trade, with towns such as Palma, Pollentia and on Menorca Mago and Iamo. Christianity was well established by the 5th century. A letter of Bishop Severus of Minorca describes the forced conversion of the Jews of Mago in 418, a rare window on island life.
balearica.e: Vandal raids from Africa struck the islands from 425. Around 455 the Vandals under Gaiseric took control, ending Roman rule. The islands passed to Byzantium after Belisarius' reconquest of Africa in 534.

barony-of-kalavryta.t: Short-lived Frankish barony in the mountains of northern Peloponnese, one of the first lost to the reviving Byzantines.
barony-of-kalavryta.o: Kalavryta was one of the twelve baronies set up in the Principality of Achaea around 1209. It was granted to Otho of Tournay and covered the mountainous district around the town of Kalavryta in the northern Peloponnese, with twelve knight's fiefs.
barony-of-kalavryta.r: Like other baronies, it was held by a French knightly family owing military service and counsel to the prince and governing a Greek peasant population from a castle. Records say little more about it than the name of its lords.
barony-of-kalavryta.e: After the Principality ceded Mistras and other forts to Byzantium in 1262, Byzantine forces pushed north. Kalavryta was taken around 1270 and the barony ceased to exist, though the area later changed hands again before passing permanently to the Despotate of the Morea.

berziti.t: Slavic tribe of western Macedonia, the Brsjaci, caught between Byzantium and Bulgaria until absorbed by the Bulgarian state in the 9th century.
berziti.o: The Berziti were among the Slavic groups that settled in Macedonia in the 7th century, in the region around Ohrid, Prilep and Bitola. Byzantine sources refer to their land as Berzitia; the later Macedonian ethnographic name Brsjaci is often traced to them.
berziti.r: Known only from a few Byzantine notices, they lived under their own chiefs (archons), at times tributary to Byzantium. In the 770s the Bulgarian ruler Telerig planned to resettle them in Bulgaria, and the Byzantine emperor Constantine V campaigned in the region.
berziti.e: During the reigns of Presian and Boris I in the mid-9th century their territory passed to the First Bulgarian Empire, and the name disappears.

bourbon-spain.t: Spain under the Bourbon dynasty from Philip V to Isabella II, a time of centralising reform, Napoleonic invasion and the loss of most of its American empire.
bourbon-spain.o: Charles II, last of Habsburg Spain, left the throne to Philip of Anjou, grandson of Louis XIV, who became Philip V in 1700. The War of the Spanish Succession confirmed him as king but cost Spain its European possessions at Utrecht in 1713, while the Nueva Planta decrees abolished the separate institutions of the Crown of Aragon.
bourbon-spain.r: The Bourbons built a more centralised state on the French model, with intendants, new academies and royal factories. Charles III (1759-1788) promoted roads, trade reform and enlightened ministers and expelled the Jesuits. The monarchy was shattered by the 1808 French invasion; Ferdinand VII then restored absolutism, and the American colonies won independence in the 1810s and 1820s.
bourbon-spain.e: Isabella II's reign was dominated by Carlist Wars, generals and court scandal. The Glorious Revolution of September 1868 drove her into exile, opening the Sexenio Democrático.

beylik-of-the-west.t: The western province of Ottoman Algiers, governed from Mazouna, Mascara and finally Oran, on the frontier with Spain and Morocco.
beylik-of-the-west.o: The Regency of Algiers created the western beylik in 1563, with its first seat at Mazouna. As the Ottomans consolidated control over the former Zayyanid Kingdom of Tlemcen, the capital moved to Mascara around 1700, closer to Spanish Oran, which the beys sought to recapture.
beylik-of-the-west.r: The beys governed the plains and highlands of western Algeria through makhzen tribes, collecting taxes in grain and livestock. Mustapha Bouchelaghem captured Oran in 1708, though Spain retook it in 1732. Mohammed el-Kebir took possession of Oran in 1792, made it his capital and built mosques there.
beylik-of-the-west.e: After the fall of Algiers in 1830, the last bey, Hassan, surrendered Oran to the French in January 1831. The western tribes soon rallied to the Emirate of Abdelkader, while the territory became part of French Algeria.

burid-emirate-of-damascus.t: The dynasty of Tughtekin that ruled Damascus for half a century, resisting both the Crusaders and the Zengids.
burid-emirate-of-damascus.o: Tughtekin, the Turkish atabeg of the Seljuk prince Duqaq, took power in Damascus after Duqaq's death in 1104. The dynasty takes its name from his son Taj al-Muluk Buri, who succeeded him in 1128.
burid-emirate-of-damascus.r: The Burids governed with the support of the Damascene notables and the urban militia. Tughtekin fought and negotiated with the Kingdom of Jerusalem, while Buri, after the Nizari Ismailis gained influence in the city, allowed a massacre of them in 1129. To resist Zengi of Aleppo, the regent Mu'in al-Din Unur allied with Jerusalem, but the Second Crusade nonetheless besieged Damascus in July 1148 and withdrew after five days.
burid-emirate-of-damascus.e: Weakened by internal rivalries, Mujir al-Din Abaq lost the support of the city, which opened its gates to Nur al-Din in April 1154, uniting Muslim Syria under the Zengid dynasty.

beylik-of-constantine.t: The eastern province of Ottoman Algiers, the largest and richest, whose last bey made Constantine the final stronghold against the French.
beylik-of-constantine.o: The Regency of Algiers organised the eastern beylik in 1567, with its seat in the ancient rock-top city of Constantine. It covered eastern Algeria from Kabylia to the Tunisian border and south to the Saharan oases such as Touggourt.
beylik-of-constantine.r: The beys ruled through local great families and makhzen tribes, collecting taxes in grain, wool and livestock and paying heavy tribute to Algiers. Salah Bey, who ruled from 1771 to 1792, built mosques, madrasas and bridges and is remembered in local song. Constantine was a centre of learning, crafts and leather work.
beylik-of-constantine.e: After Algiers fell in 1830, Ahmed Bey held Constantine and repulsed a French assault in 1836. The French stormed the city in October 1837, and the beylik was absorbed into French Algeria; Ahmed Bey fought on until 1848.

bishopric-of-pomesania.t: Prussian prince-bishopric on the lower Vistula, closely tied to the Teutonic Order, whose bishop embraced the Reformation in the 1520s.
bishopric-of-pomesania.o: The diocese was one of four created in Prussia by William of Modena in 1243, covering the land of the Pomesanians. The bishop received a third of the territory as his own principality, with the castle of Riesenburg (Prabuty) as residence and a cathedral at Marienwerder (Kwidzyn).
bishopric-of-pomesania.r: Its cathedral chapter belonged to the Teutonic Order from 1285, and the bishops were usually loyal to the Order. Marienwerder became the centre of the cult of Dorothea of Montau, a local mystic. After 1466 the bishopric remained in the Order's part of Prussia, under Polish overlordship.
bishopric-of-pomesania.e: Bishop Erhard von Queis adopted Lutheranism and, after the secularisation of the Order's state into Ducal Prussia in 1525, surrendered his secular rule to Duke Albert in 1527. The territory became part of Ducal Prussia, and the Protestant bishopric was later abolished.

bastetani.t: An Iberian people of the Granada highlands, whose capital Basti yielded the seated stone goddess known as the Lady of Baza.
bastetani.o: The Bastetani occupied the uplands of eastern Andalusia, in modern Granada, Almería and Jaén, from the mid-first millennium BCE. Their main town was Basti, near Baza, and they bordered the Oretani, Contestani and coastal Bastuli.
bastetani.r: They lived in fortified towns on hills controlling routes between the coast and the Guadalquivir valley. Their elites were buried in rich chamber tombs, as at Tútugi (Galera) and Basti, where the Lady of Baza, a painted stone statue of an enthroned woman used as a cinerary urn, was found in 1971. Their economy combined farming, herding and esparto working.
bastetani.e: After Carthaginian control, the Bastetani passed under Rome during the Second Punic War and joined the great revolt of 197 BCE before being pacified. Their region was divided between Hispania Citerior and Baetica in Roman times.

beylik-of-chaka.t: The Aegean emirate of Chaka Bey, the first Turkish ruler to build a fleet and threaten Constantinople from the sea.
beylik-of-chaka.o: Chaka, called Tzachas by the Byzantines, was a Turkish commander who had been a captive at the Byzantine court of Nikephoros III. After his release he seized Smyrna and the Aegean coast of western Anatolia, probably in the late 1080s.
beylik-of-chaka.r: With Greek shipwrights he built a fleet, took Phocaea, Clazomenae and the islands of Lesbos, Chios and Samos, and styled himself emperor. In 1090-1091 he allied with the Pechenegs, who were then besieging Constantinople, but the Byzantine navy and the Pecheneg defeat at Levounion in 1091 ended the threat. Little is known of his government.
beylik-of-chaka.e: Alexios I persuaded Chaka's son-in-law, the Rum Seljuk Kilij Arslan I, to kill him at a banquet around 1093. After the First Crusade, the Byzantine general John Doukas recovered Smyrna in 1097-1098.

barcid-iberia.t: The Carthaginian domain built in Iberia by Hamilcar Barca and his heirs, the silver-rich base from which Hannibal set out to invade Italy.
barcid-iberia.o: After losing Sicily in the First Punic War, Carthage sent Hamilcar Barca to Iberia in 237 BCE. Landing at Gadir, he conquered the Guadalquivir valley and its mines. After his death in about 229 BCE, his son-in-law Hasdrubal extended Carthaginian power by diplomacy and founded Qart Hadasht, later Carthago Nova, around 227 BCE.
barcid-iberia.r: Barcid Iberia was run almost as a family dominion of the Barcids, nominally under Carthage. Silver from mines near Qart Hadasht and the Sierra Morena paid for armies of Iberian, Celtiberian and African troops. Alliances with local rulers were sealed by marriages, such as Hannibal's to Himilce of Castulo. In 226 BCE the Ebro treaty with Rome fixed a northern limit.
barcid-iberia.e: Hannibal, in command from 221 BCE, took Saguntum in 219 BCE, starting the Second Punic War. Scipio captured Qart Hadasht in 209 BCE and won at Ilipa in 206 BCE, ending Carthaginian rule. The territory became the Roman provinces of Hispania Citerior and Ulterior.

bremen-soviet-republic.t: Council republic in the port city of Bremen in early 1919, suppressed after a few weeks by government troops.
bremen-soviet-republic.o: After the November revolution of 1918, workers' and soldiers' councils took power in Bremen. On 10 January 1919, after the Spartacist rising in Berlin, left-wing radicals and Communists proclaimed a Soviet Republic, dissolving the city's senate and parliament.
bremen-soviet-republic.r: The council government, dominated by Communists and Independent Socialists, controlled the city for less than a month. It faced shortages of money and food, as banks refused credit, and opposition from the middle classes and moderate Social Democrats. Its leaders tried to negotiate with the national government but refused to disarm.
bremen-soviet-republic.e: On 4 February 1919 the Freikorps Division Gerstenberg, sent by Gustav Noske, stormed Bremen. About 80 people died, and the Soviet Republic ended. Bremen resumed as a city-state within the Weimar Republic.

barony-of-vostitsa.t: Barony of the Principality of Achaea on the Gulf of Corinth, centred on Vostitsa, the modern Aigio.
barony-of-vostitsa.o: After the Frankish conquest of the Peloponnese, the Principality of Achaea was divided into twelve baronies around 1209. Vostitsa, with a modest number of knight's fiefs, was granted to the Charpigny family from Burgundy, who held it through the 13th century.
barony-of-vostitsa.r: The barons held the castle and town on the south shore of the Gulf of Corinth, owed military service to the prince and sat in his high court, while Greek villagers farmed the land under them. Little detail of daily government survives beyond mentions in the Chronicle of the Morea and Angevin records.
barony-of-vostitsa.e: In the 14th century the barony passed by inheritance and sale among the Enghien and other lords, and became involved in the struggles of the Navarrese Company. It was eventually lost to the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea in the early 15th century, as the principality crumbled.

bangwaketse-chiefdom.t: A Tswana chiefdom centred on Kanye whose rulers helped secure British protection rather than Company rule for Botswana.
bangwaketse-chiefdom.o: The Bangwaketse separated from the Bakwena in the 18th century and settled in south-eastern Botswana. Under Makaba II in the late 18th and early 19th centuries they became one of the strongest Tswana states, until Makaba was killed in 1824 during the wars of that era.
bangwaketse-chiefdom.r: Chiefs ruled from a large town through ward heads and the kgotla, drawing wealth from cattle and trade in ivory and skins with the Cape. After years of displacement, Gaseitsiwe re-established the chiefdom at Kanye, a defensible hill town. Missionaries of the London Missionary Society were influential.
bangwaketse-chiefdom.e: The chiefdom joined the Bechuanaland Protectorate in 1885. In 1895 Bathoen I travelled to London with Khama III and Sebele I to oppose transfer to the British South Africa Company, and the protectorate was preserved. Ngwaketse is now a district of Botswana.

bagratid-armenia.t: The medieval Armenian kingdom of the Bagratids, whose capital Ani became famous as the city of a thousand and one churches.
bagratid-armenia.o: Ashot Bagratuni, recognised as prince of princes in 862, received a royal crown from the Abbasid caliph around 884 with Byzantine approval, reviving the Armenian monarchy after more than four centuries. The kingdom grew out of the Principality of Armenia and the family's vast estates in Shirak and Ayrarat.
bagratid-armenia.r: The kingdom was a federation of noble houses and rival kingdoms under the Bagratid king of kings. Smbat I was executed by the Sajid emir Yusuf in 914, but Ashot II the Iron restored royal power. Ashot III moved the capital to Ani in 961, which grew wealthy on trade between Byzantium and Iran. Under Gagik I the architect Trdat completed Ani Cathedral in 1001.
bagratid-armenia.e: Hovhannes-Smbat bequeathed his kingdom to Byzantium, and in 1045 Gagik II was forced to surrender Ani to the Byzantine Empire. The Seljuks sacked Ani in 1064, and many Armenians moved west towards Cilicia.

barony-of-patras.t: The largest barony of the Principality of Achaea, centred on the port of Patras, later sold to its Latin archbishop.
barony-of-patras.o: When the Principality of Achaea was organised around 1209, Patras, the main port of the north-western Peloponnese, was granted as a barony with 24 knight's fiefs to William Aleman, a knight possibly of German or Provencal origin. He fortified the ancient citadel above the town.
barony-of-patras.r: The barons held the castle and city, owed service to the prince and shared the town with the Latin archbishop, who was the senior Catholic prelate in the principality. Patras was a commercial centre for silk, currants and trade with Italy, with a Greek majority under Latin lords.
barony-of-patras.e: Over the 13th century the archbishops acquired the baronial rights. Around 1276 the barony passed to the archbishop, creating the Latin Archbishopric of Patras, a church-ruled state that lasted until 1430.

bit-adini.t: Bit Adini, an Aramaean kingdom on the Euphrates bend whose fall in 856 BCE opened Syria to Assyrian armies.
bit-adini.o: After the Late Bronze Age collapse, Til Barsip at Tell Ahmar was the Luwian city of Masuwari. In the 10th century BCE Aramaean tribes took control, and the land on both banks of the Euphrates became Bit Adini, the House of Adini, controlling a key river crossing.
bit-adini.r: Bit Adini combined Aramaean tribal leadership with older Luwian urban traditions, and its rulers raised fortified towns. King Ahuni led resistance to Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III of the Assyrian Empire, forming alliances with Carchemish and other Syrian kingdoms.
bit-adini.e: Shalmaneser III captured Til Barsip in 856 BCE, renamed it Kar-Shalmaneser and made it an Assyrian base, with palaces decorated with wall paintings. Ahuni was deported to Assyria.

byzantine-spania.t: The East Roman foothold on Spain's south-east coast, won by Justinian in 552 and held for some seventy years against the Visigoths.
byzantine-spania.o: In 552 the Visigothic noble Athanagild, rebelling against King Agila, sought help from Justinian. An imperial force under the elderly patrician Liberius landed in the south-east, and in the following years the Byzantines seized a coastal strip from around Cartagena to Málaga and beyond, organised as the province of Spania.
byzantine-spania.r: Spania was run by a magister militum based at Carthago Nova, and an inscription of 589 records the governor Comenciolus repairing the city's defences. It formed part of Justinian's restoration of the Roman Empire in the West, linked to Byzantine Africa. Its population was Hispano-Roman and Catholic, and Byzantine authority was mainly military and fiscal.
byzantine-spania.e: Visigothic kings steadily pushed the Byzantines back. Leovigild retook inland areas, Sisebut captured Málaga around 615, and Suintila expelled the last imperial forces around 624. Carthago Nova was destroyed in the fighting.

bruttii.t: Oscan-speaking people who broke away from the Lucanians in 356 BCE and dominated the toe of Italy, Hannibal's last stronghold.
bruttii.o: Diodorus says that in 356 BCE runaway slaves and herdsmen in the mountains of Calabria, then under Lucanian control, rebelled and formed a new people, the Bruttii. The story may simplify a revolt of a subject population, but by the late 4th century BCE they were an independent federation.
bruttii.r: Their capital was Consentia (Cosenza). They lived in hill towns and drew wealth from the Sila forest, producing pitch and timber. They captured Greek cities including Hipponion and Terina and minted fine coins. They fought Alexander of Epirus and joined Pyrrhus against Rome.
bruttii.e: Rome subdued them by 270 BCE and took half the Sila. They joined Hannibal after Cannae, and Bruttium was his last base in Italy until he left in 203 BCE. As punishment they lost land and status; Roman writers said they were reduced to serving as attendants to magistrates.

bara-kingdom.t: The cattle-herding Bara people of southern-central Madagascar, ruled by Zafimanely nobles in several rival kingdoms.
bara-kingdom.o: The Bara occupied the grasslands of south-central Madagascar around Ihosy, where a ruling house, the Zafimanely, established authority over cattle-herding clans by the 17th century. Tradition links the Zafimanely to the dynasties of the south-east.
bara-kingdom.r: Bara society was organised around cattle, which measured wealth and were central to ritual, and around warrior values, including cattle raiding as a test of manhood. Power was divided among several Zafimanely chiefs rather than a single state. Little written evidence exists before the 19th century.
bara-kingdom.e: The Merina Kingdom established posts in Bara country in the 19th century but never fully controlled it. French forces subdued the region around 1900. The Bara remain one of Madagascar's main pastoral peoples.

bailiwick-of-jersey.t: The largest Channel Island, a self-governing Crown Dependency that has stayed loyal to the English crown since the loss of Normandy in 1204.
bailiwick-of-jersey.o: Jersey was part of the Duchy of Normandy from 933. After King John lost mainland Normandy in 1204, the island remained with the English crown and became a separate bailiwick under a warden, later a lieutenant governor, with a bailiff heading its Royal Court.
bailiwick-of-jersey.r: Jersey kept Norman customary law and its own States assembly. Mont Orgueil Castle defended it against frequent French attacks. The island traded in cod from Newfoundland, knitted woollens and later potatoes and cattle, and grew into a financial centre. Charles II was proclaimed king there in 1649, and the French were defeated at the Battle of Jersey in 1781.
bailiwick-of-jersey.e: Germany occupied Jersey from 1940 to 1945. Today it is a Crown Dependency outside the United Kingdom, with its own parliament, the States Assembly, and its own laws and taxes.

banate-of-severin.t: Hungarian frontier province at the Iron Gates of the Danube, a defensive march against Bulgarians, Cumans and later the Ottomans.
banate-of-severin.o: King Andrew II's son Béla set up the banate around 1228–1233, in lands taken from Bulgaria and the Cumans east of the Iron Gates, around the fortress of Severin (Drobeta-Turnu Severin) built on Roman ruins. In 1247 Béla IV granted it to the Knights Hospitaller, though they soon left.
banate-of-severin.r: A royal ban commanded the castle and the border, collecting tribute from the Romanian voivodes and knezes beyond, such as the Voivodeship of Litovoi. Control shifted repeatedly with Bulgaria and later the Principality of Wallachia, whose rulers took the title ban of Severin. In the 15th century Hungary held it against the Ottomans, and John Hunyadi was ban.
banate-of-severin.e: Ottoman raids steadily wore it down. Severin fortress fell to the Ottomans in 1524, two years before Mohács, and the banate ceased to exist. The region passed to Wallachia as Oltenia's western edge.

bosporan-kingdom.t: Long-lived Greek kingdom on the Kerch Strait that fed Athens with Black Sea grain and survived as a Roman client state until the coming of the Huns.
bosporan-kingdom.o: Greek colonies on both sides of the Cimmerian Bosporus, such as Panticapaeum, Phanagoria and Theodosia, united under the Archaeanactid dynasty around 480 BCE. In 438 BCE power passed to Spartocus I, whose Spartocid descendants ruled for more than three centuries from Panticapaeum, modern Kerch, extending control over local Sindians and Maeotians.
bosporan-kingdom.r: The Spartocids called themselves archons of the Greek cities and kings of the native peoples. Wealth came from grain, fish and slaves shipped to the Aegean: Leucon I (389-349 BCE) granted Athens tax-free grain purchases and was honoured there. Rich kurgan burials show a blend of Greek and Scythian and Sarmatian culture.
bosporan-kingdom.e: Under pressure from the Scythians, Paerisades V handed the kingdom to Mithridates VI of Pontus c. 108 BCE. Later kings, such as Aspurgus and his successors, ruled as clients of Rome. The kingdom declined in the 3rd century CE and was overrun by the Huns in the 370s.
bosporan-kingdom.re: Ancient Greek religion, later also Christianity and Judaism

bit-bahiani.t: Bit Bahiani, an Aramaean kingdom of the upper Khabur centred on Guzana, famous for the sculpted palace of King Kapara at Tell Halaf.
bit-bahiani.o: Aramaean tribes took over the upper Khabur in the 10th century BCE, and the House of Bahiani ruled from Guzana, at Tell Halaf on the Syrian-Turkish border. In 894 BCE its king Abi-salamu paid tribute to Adad-nirari II of the Assyrian Empire.
bit-bahiani.r: King Kapara built a palace whose facade had colossal statues of gods on animals and dozens of carved stone reliefs. Excavated by Max von Oppenheim from 1911, they were shattered by bombing in Berlin in 1943 and painstakingly restored. A bilingual statue of the ruler Hadad-yith'i in Assyrian and Aramaic shows the kingdom adapting to Assyrian rule.
bit-bahiani.e: Bit Bahiani became an Assyrian vassal and finally a province c. 808 BCE. Guzana is the Gozan of the Bible, where Israelites were deported after the fall of Samaria.

bibroci.t: British people named only once by Julius Caesar, among the groups that surrendered to him during his second invasion in 54 BCE.
bibroci.o: Known only from Caesar's Gallic War, the Bibroci were one of five British peoples, with the Cenimagni, Segontiaci, Ancalites and Cassi, who sent envoys to surrender to him in 54 BCE after the Trinovantes had come under his protection.
bibroci.r: Nothing is recorded of their government, rulers or way of life. Their territory is unknown; scholars have suggested places in the Thames valley or in Berkshire and Sussex, but no inscription or coin securely names them.
bibroci.e: They vanish from the record after Caesar's account. Their land was presumably absorbed by larger neighbours such as the Atrebates (Britain) or the Catuvellauni before the Roman conquest of 43.

basutoland.t: The British territory that preserved Moshoeshoe's mountain kingdom from absorption into South Africa, and became independent Lesotho.
basutoland.o: At Moshoeshoe's request, Britain annexed the Basotho Kingdom in March 1868 to save it from the Orange Free State. In 1871 it was handed to the Cape Colony.
basutoland.r: Cape attempts to disarm the Basotho caused the Gun War of 1880-1881, which the Basotho effectively won, and in 1884 Britain resumed direct rule as a High Commission territory from Maseru. Paramount chiefs of Moshoeshoe's line, among them Letsie I and Lerotholi, kept wide authority, and a Basutoland National Council was created in 1903. Hut tax and poor land made the territory a labour reserve for South African mines.
basutoland.e: Basutoland was never incorporated into South Africa. After the rise of parties such as the Basutoland Congress Party and constitutional reforms, it became independent as the Kingdom of Lesotho on 4 October 1966 under Moshoeshoe II.

barolong-chiefdom.t: One of the oldest Tswana chiefdoms, whose branches at Thaba Nchu and Mafikeng were drawn into the struggles between Boers and Britain.
barolong-chiefdom.o: The Barolong are among the oldest Tswana groups, settled in the southern Kalahari margins and the Molopo valley. Under the 18th-century ruler Tau they became a powerful chiefdom, but after his death they split into branches, chief among them the Ratlou, Tshidi, Seleka and Rapulana.
barolong-chiefdom.r: Chiefs ruled large towns through ward headmen and the kgotla assembly, with cattle herding and cereal farming as the economy. During the wars of the 1820s the Seleka under Moroka moved to Thaba Nchu, where they aided the Voortrekkers in 1836. Methodist missionaries had a strong influence. The Tshidi under Montshiwa settled at Mafikeng and resisted Boer encroachment.
barolong-chiefdom.e: Conflict with the Boer statelets of Stellaland and Goshen led Britain to intervene, and in 1885 Barolong lands were divided between British Bechuanaland and the Bechuanaland Protectorate. Mafikeng later became famous for its siege in the Second Boer War.

barony-of-passavant.t: Frankish barony in the Mani held by the marshals of Achaea, whose castle of Passava watched over the unruly Maniots.
barony-of-passavant.o: Around 1220 John of Neuilly, hereditary marshal of the Principality of Achaea, received a fief at the entrance to the Mani peninsula and built a castle there called Passavant, now Passava, near Gytheio. Its purpose was to control the independent-minded population of the Mani and the route into Laconia.
barony-of-passavant.r: The barony was small but held by one of the great officers of the principality, the marshal, who commanded the army. Its lords ruled from the castle over Greek villages, alongside the castle of Grand Magne built by William II of Villehardouin further south.
barony-of-passavant.e: After William II was captured at Pelagonia in 1259, he ceded Mistras, Monemvasia and Grand Magne to Byzantium, and Passavant was lost to the Byzantines soon after, around 1263. The Neuilly heiress Margaret of Passavant later claimed Akova.

banate-of-bosnia.t: Medieval Bosnian state ruled by bans under nominal Hungarian overlordship, known for its silver mines and its own Bosnian Church.
banate-of-bosnia.o: Bosnia appears as a distinct land in the 10th century. In 1154 Ban Borić is the first named ruler, a vassal of Hungary. Ban Kulin (c. 1180–1204) made it effectively independent, and his 1189 trade charter to Ragusa is one of the oldest documents in the Serbian-Croatian language.
banate-of-bosnia.r: The ban ruled with a council of nobles from seats around Visoko. The Bosnian Church, an independent church condemned by Rome as heretical, coexisted with Catholicism and Orthodoxy. Under Stephen II Kotromanić (1322–1353) Bosnia annexed Zachlumia and the land up to the Cetina, and Saxon miners opened silver and lead mines at Srebrenica and Fojnica, trading through Ragusa.
banate-of-bosnia.e: In 1377 Ban Tvrtko I had himself crowned king at Mile, claiming the Serbian crown as well, and the banate became the Kingdom of Bosnia.

bishopric-of-courland.t: Prince-bishopric in western Latvia, founded during the conquest of the Curonians, whose remnant survived as the District of Pilten.
bishopric-of-courland.o: The papal legate Baldwin of Alna created a bishopric for the Curonians in 1234 after treaties with Curonian leaders. When Courland was conquered by the Livonian Order in the 1250s and 1260s, the bishop received about a third of the land, scattered in several districts.
bishopric-of-courland.r: The bishop's lands centred on Pilten and Hasenpoth, with the cathedral at Hasenpoth (Aizpute). Unlike other Livonian bishops, those of Courland were closely tied to the Livonian Order, and the chapter was for a time made up of Order priests. Curonian and Latvian peasants worked the estates of German vassals.
bishopric-of-courland.e: In 1559 Bishop Johann von Münchhausen sold the bishopric to Frederick II of Denmark, who gave it to his brother Magnus of Holstein. After Magnus died in 1583, Denmark sold its rights to Poland-Lithuania in 1585, and the territory became the District of Pilten.

barotseland.t: The Lozi kingdom of the upper Zambezi floodplain, ruled by the Litunga, which kept a special status under British rule until Zambian independence.
barotseland.o: The Luyi (later Lozi) people settled the Bulozi floodplain of the upper Zambezi, with traditions linking their first ruler, Mbuyu, to the Lunda world. By the 17th century the Litunga headed a centralised kingdom that drew on the floodplain's fish, cattle and cultivated mounds.
barotseland.r: The Litunga ruled through a council (kuta) of titled officials and a system of state-owned labour and tribute, and moved his court each year from the flooding plain to higher ground in the Kuomboka ceremony. Mulambwa reformed the law in the early 19th century. From about 1840 the kingdom was conquered by the Makololo under Sebitwane, but Sipopa restored Lozi rule in 1864.
barotseland.e: Lewanika signed a concession with the British South Africa Company in 1890, and Barotseland became a protectorate within Northern Rhodesia with its own institutions. The 1964 Barotseland Agreement merged it into independent Zambia, a settlement still disputed today.

belegezites.t: Slavic tribe settled in Thessaly in the 7th century, remembered for trading grain with besieged Thessalonica.
belegezites.o: The Belegezites were one of the Slavic groups that settled in the Balkans during the great migrations of the late 6th and 7th centuries. They occupied lands in Thessaly around Phthiotic Thebes and Demetrias on the Gulf of Volos. Almost everything known about them comes from the Miracles of Saint Demetrius, a Byzantine collection of stories about Thessalonica.
belegezites.r: They lived as farming communities under their own chiefs, partly independent of Byzantium. During the Slavic siege of Thessalonica in the 670s they did not join the attackers but sold grain to the starving city, a sign of their prosperity and pragmatic relations with the Byzantines. Their name survives in later Byzantine sources as the region of Velegezitia.
belegezites.e: Over the 8th and 9th centuries Byzantium reasserted control over Greece through the theme system, and the Belegezites were gradually brought under imperial administration, converted to Christianity and absorbed into the Greek-speaking population. They leave few traces apart from place names.
belegezites.re: Slavic paganism, later Eastern Orthodox Christianity

barony-of-chalandritsa.t: Small Frankish barony in the hills south of Patras, one of the original fiefs of the Principality of Achaea.
barony-of-chalandritsa.o: Chalandritsa was among the baronies created in the Principality of Achaea around 1209. It was granted to Robert de la Tremouille, a knight from France, and held a small number of knight's fiefs in the hill country of Achaea south of Patras.
barony-of-chalandritsa.r: The barons owed military service to the prince and had seats in his high court. The Dramelay family later held it for much of the 13th and 14th centuries. Beyond these facts, recorded in the Chronicle of the Morea and Angevin documents, little is known of the barony's internal life.
barony-of-chalandritsa.e: In the final collapse of the principality, Chalandritsa was taken by the Byzantines of the Despotate of the Morea, under Constantine Palaiologos, in 1429, at the same time as the campaign that won Patras.

bourbon-restoration.t: The return of the Bourbon kings after Napoleon, a constitutional monarchy under Louis XVIII and Charles X that ended in the July Revolution of 1830.
bourbon-restoration.o: After Napoleon's abdication in April 1814 the allies and the French Senate restored Louis XVIII, brother of Louis XVI. He granted the Charter of 1814, which kept a parliament and many revolutionary gains. Napoleon's return in the Hundred Days of 1815 interrupted the regime until Waterloo.
bourbon-restoration.r: France had a two-chamber parliament elected by a very small, wealthy electorate. Moderate ministers such as the Duke of Richelieu paid off war indemnities and ended the allied occupation in 1818, while ultra-royalists pressed for revenge after the White Terror. Charles X, crowned at Reims in 1825, compensated émigrés and favoured the Church.
bourbon-restoration.e: In July 1830 Charles X issued ordinances dissolving parliament and curbing the press. Three days of revolt in Paris drove him into exile, and Louis-Philippe of Orléans became king, beginning the July Monarchy. Algiers had been taken weeks earlier.

banu-qasi.t: A Muslim dynasty of Visigothic descent that dominated the upper Ebro for two centuries, allied by blood with the kings of Pamplona.
banu-qasi.o: The Banu Qasi claimed descent from a Visigothic count called Cassius who converted to Islam after the conquest of 711 to 714, keeping his lands in the upper Ebro valley. As muwallads, native Muslims, they became the leading family of the Upper March, based at Tudela.
banu-qasi.r: They balanced between Córdoba, the Franks and the Christian kingdoms, intermarrying with the Arista family of Pamplona, whose founder Íñigo Arista was a half-brother of Musa ibn Musa. Musa ruled Tudela, Zaragoza and Huesca and was called the third king of Spain, until Ordoño I of Asturias defeated him at Albelda in 859. Later family members fought Córdoba, the Tujibids and Navarre.
banu-qasi.e: Weakened by family divisions and wars with Sancho Garcés I of Pamplona, the dynasty lost Tudela and its lands. Abd al-Rahman III ended its power in the 920s, and the Tujibid family took over the Upper March.

balaton-principality.t: Frankish vassal principality around Lake Balaton where Pribina and Kocel built churches and welcomed Methodius's Slavonic liturgy.
balaton-principality.o: Pribina, a Slavic prince expelled from Nitra by Mojmir I of Moravia around 833, entered Frankish service. Around 839 Louis the German granted him lands in Lower Pannonia, and he built a fortified seat at Mosapurc (Zalavár) on the Zala river near Lake Balaton.
balaton-principality.r: Pribina ruled as a Frankish vassal, settling Slavs and Bavarians and founding some 30 churches consecrated by the archbishops of Salzburg. Under his son Kocel, Mosapurc was an important church centre. In 867 Kocel welcomed Cyril and Methodius and supported the Slavonic liturgy, and Methodius was made archbishop of Pannonia in 870.
balaton-principality.e: Pribina was killed fighting Moravians in 861. After Kocel's death around 876 the principality returned to direct Frankish rule, and the Hungarian conquest of the 890s ended Frankish power in Pannonia.

british-seychelles.t: The Indian Ocean archipelago held by Britain from the Napoleonic Wars until 1976, a plantation colony and a place of exile.
british-seychelles.o: The French-settled Seychelles surrendered to British warships several times during the Napoleonic Wars, while the French commandant Quéau de Quinssy stayed on to run the islands. After the capture of Mauritius in 1810 they passed under British control, confirmed by the Treaty of Paris in 1814, and were governed as a dependency of Mauritius.
british-seychelles.r: French-speaking planters grew cotton and then coconuts, cinnamon and vanilla with enslaved labour until abolition in 1835; Africans freed from slave ships by the Royal Navy were later landed there. A Creole society formed, mostly Catholic. The islands became a separate Crown colony in 1903 with its capital at Victoria, and served as a place of exile for figures such as Prempeh I of Asante and Archbishop Makarios of Cyprus.
british-seychelles.e: Independence came on 29 June 1976 under President James Mancham, whose government was overthrown in a coup the next year by France-Albert René.

brigantes-ireland.t: People of south-east Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, bearing the same name as the great Brigantes confederation of northern Britain.
brigantes-ireland.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 lists the Brigantes in south-eastern Ireland, usually placed in the area of modern Wexford and Waterford, near the Coriondi and the Usdiae. The name, meaning roughly 'the high ones' or linked to the goddess Brigantia, is the same as that of the Brigantes of northern Britain.
brigantes-ireland.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. The shared name has encouraged theories of migration from Britain to Ireland, or of a common cult of a goddess later remembered as Brigit, but there is no evidence beyond the name. The south-east coast faced Wales and Gaul and was open to sea trade.
brigantes-ireland.e: The Irish Brigantes vanish from the record after Ptolemy. Their area later lay within the Kingdom of Leinster, the Kingdom of Osraige and the lands of the Deisi Muman.

banat-of-craiova.t: Habsburg-ruled Oltenia, the western third of Wallachia, held by Austria for two decades after the Treaty of Passarowitz.
banat-of-craiova.o: In the Austro-Turkish war of 1716 to 1718 Habsburg forces occupied Oltenia, the part of Wallachia west of the Olt river. The Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 ceded it to the Habsburg monarchy, which organised it as a province with its seat at Craiova, the traditional residence of the Wallachian bans.
banat-of-craiova.r: The province was governed by an imperial administration with a local boyar, Gheorghe Cantacuzino, as ban at first. Vienna introduced a census, regular taxes, a postal service and stricter control over boyars and monasteries, reforms that curbed noble privileges but raised burdens; many peasants fled across the Olt. Orthodox religion and Romanian-speaking society remained unchanged.
banat-of-craiova.e: Habsburg defeat in the war of 1737 to 1739 led to the Treaty of Belgrade in 1739, which returned Oltenia to Wallachia under Ottoman suzerainty. The episode left detailed Austrian maps and surveys of the region.

banat-of-temeswar.t: Habsburg crown domain in the plain of the Banat, run directly from Vienna as a laboratory of colonisation and drainage after its conquest from the Ottomans.
banat-of-temeswar.o: Prince Eugene of Savoy captured Temeswar from the Ottomans in 1716, and the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 confirmed Habsburg possession of the Banat between the Mureș, Tisza and Danube. Rather than returning it to Hungary, Charles VI kept it as a crown domain under military and court administration.
banat-of-temeswar.r: Governor Claudius Florimund Mercy rebuilt Temeswar as a baroque fortress town, drained marshes, dug the Bega canal and promoted rice, silk and mining. Tens of thousands of Catholic German settlers, later called Danube Swabians, were brought in alongside Serbs, Romanians and Italians, while Hungarian nobles were largely excluded. The Banat was governed by a provincial administration answering to Vienna.
banat-of-temeswar.e: In 1778 Maria Theresa returned the civil Banat to Hungary as the counties of Temes, Torontál and Krassó, while its southern strip stayed in the Military Frontier. Its mixed population shaped the region until it was divided between Romania, Yugoslavia and Hungary in 1920.

broerec.t: Breton kingdom of the Vannes region, named the land of Waroch after a warlord who defied the Franks.
broerec.o: In the 6th century Breton rulers extended their power over the Vannetais, the former land of the Veneti, which remained largely Gallo-Roman. Gregory of Tours records the counts Macliau and his son Waroch fighting for control of Vannes.
broerec.r: Waroch repeatedly raided Frankish territory around Rennes and Nantes and defeated or bought off Frankish armies sent by Guntram and Chilperic I in the 570s and 580s. The region kept a strong Gallo-Roman element alongside the Breton settlers, and Vannes remained a bishopric.
broerec.e: Broërec remained the border zone between the Bretons and the Franks until it was absorbed into the Kingdom of Brittany created by Nominoe, who was count of Vannes for Louis the Pious. Its name survives in the Breton name of the Vannes region.

bishopric-of-dorpat.t: Prince-bishopric of south-eastern Estonia centred on Dorpat (Tartu), a prosperous Hanseatic frontier facing Pskov, until Ivan the Terrible took it in 1558.
bishopric-of-dorpat.o: Hermann of Buxhoeveden, brother of Bishop Albert of Riga, became bishop of the Estonians in 1220 and moved his see to Dorpat after its capture in 1224. The bishopric took over the former lands of Ugandi, Vaiga and Mõhu, and Hermann received them as a prince of the Holy Roman Empire.
bishopric-of-dorpat.r: The bishop ruled through a cathedral chapter and German vassals, sharing power with the Livonian Order and the diets of Terra Mariana. Dorpat, a Hanseatic member, grew rich from trade with Pskov and Novgorod and built a large Gothic cathedral. Estonian peasants worked the land under increasing serfdom.
bishopric-of-dorpat.e: At the start of the Livonian War Ivan IV of Russia took Dorpat in 1558, and the last bishop, Hermann Wesel, was taken to Russia, where he died. The territory was later contested by Poland-Lithuania and Sweden, and passed to Swedish Livonia in the 1620s.

belli.t: The Celtiberian people of Segeda, whose new city walls provoked the Roman war of 153 BCE and so moved the start of the Roman year to January.
belli.o: The Belli lived in the Jalón and Huerva valleys of modern Zaragoza province from about the 4th century BCE, part of the wider Celtiberian world. Their towns included Segeda and Contrebia Belaisca, the modern Botorrita.
belli.r: They lived in walled towns with councils of elders and magistrates. The Botorrita bronzes, the longest texts in the Celtiberian language, come from Contrebia Belaisca and record local regulations, while a Latin bronze from the same site records a Roman arbitration of 87 BCE. Their economy rested on farming, herding and metalworking.
belli.e: In 154 BCE Segeda enlarged its walls, which Rome treated as a breach of treaty. To send an army quickly, Rome began the consular year on 1 January 153 BCE. Led by Carus of Segeda, the Celtiberians defeated the consul Nobilior, but after Numantia fell in 133 BCE the Belli were absorbed into Hispania Citerior.

bulgaria.t: Present-day Bulgaria, a parliamentary republic since 1990 and member of NATO and the European Union.
bulgaria.o: After Todor Zhivkov's fall in November 1989 ended the dominance of the People's Republic of Bulgaria's communist party, Round Table talks led to free elections in 1990. The country was renamed the Republic of Bulgaria in November 1990, and a democratic constitution was adopted in July 1991. The philosopher Zhelyu Zhelev became the first directly elected president.
bulgaria.r: Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic with a single-chamber National Assembly. The transition was painful: a banking collapse and hyperinflation in 1996 to 1997 led to a currency board pegging the lev. The former tsar Simeon II became prime minister in 2001 as Simeon Saxe-Coburg-Gotha. Corruption and weak institutions remain central political issues.
bulgaria.e: Bulgaria joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007. Boyko Borisov dominated politics from 2009 until mass protests in 2020, followed by repeated snap elections. The country fully joined the Schengen area in 2025 and adopted the euro in 2026.

bavarian-soviet-republic.t: Short-lived council republic in Munich in April 1919, crushed by government troops and Freikorps in a wave of violence.
bavarian-soviet-republic.o: After the murder of Bavarian premier Kurt Eisner in February 1919, the elected government of Johannes Hoffmann fled Munich to Bamberg. On 6-7 April 1919 a council republic was proclaimed by writers and anarchists, including Ernst Toller, Erich Mühsam and Gustav Landauer.
bavarian-soviet-republic.r: The first council government was chaotic; within a week the Communists under Eugen Leviné took over and formed a Red Army. They decreed the socialisation of banks and industry and seized hostages. Supplies to Munich broke down. The killing of hostages at the Luitpold Gymnasium on 30 April inflamed opinion against the regime.
bavarian-soviet-republic.e: Government troops and Freikorps units entered Munich on 1-3 May 1919, killing several hundred people, including Landauer. Leviné was executed. The episode pushed Bavarian politics sharply to the right.

beylik-of-titteri.t: The smallest of the three provinces of Ottoman Algiers, governed from Médéa by beys who controlled the highlands south of the capital.
beylik-of-titteri.o: The Regency of Algiers organised its territory in the mid-16th century into the provinces of the East, the West and Titteri, with the area around Algiers itself ruled directly. Titteri, created around 1548, covered the Tell Atlas and high plains south of Algiers, with Médéa as its seat.
beylik-of-titteri.r: The bey, appointed by Algiers, collected taxes from tribes and farmers, relying on Janissary garrisons and allied makhzen tribes. Every few years he travelled to Algiers to deliver tribute in person. The province supplied grain, livestock and wool to the capital, and Médéa was a market town with Andalusi and Ottoman influences.
beylik-of-titteri.e: After the French captured Algiers in 1830, the bey Mustapha Boumezrag first submitted and then resisted. French troops occupied Médéa in late 1830, and the beylik was dissolved into French Algeria.

berbice.t: A Dutch plantation colony on the Berbice river in Guyana, remembered above all for the great slave uprising of 1763.
berbice.o: In 1627 the Zeeland merchant Abraham van Peere received a charter from the Dutch West India Company to settle the Berbice river. The colony began as a trading post at Fort Nassau upriver and was run as a private patroonship by the van Peere family.
berbice.r: Berbice developed sugar, coffee and cotton plantations worked by enslaved Africans. After a French raid in 1712, the colony was ransomed and from 1720 run by the Society of Berbice, a company of investors. In 1763 enslaved people led by Coffy rose up, controlled most of the colony for nearly a year and were suppressed only with outside troops. New Amsterdam later became the capital.
berbice.e: Britain occupied Berbice from 1796 and gained it formally in 1814. In 1831 it was merged with Demerara-Essequibo to form British Guiana. Coffy is Guyana's national hero, and 23 February, the start of the uprising, is the country's Republic Day.

boeotian-league.t: Federal state of the Boeotian cities under Theban leadership, which briefly made Thebes the strongest power in Greece after Leuctra in 371 BCE.
boeotian-league.o: The cities of Boeotia shared a dialect, cults and a sense of kinship, and by the late 6th century BCE Thebes was gathering them into a federation, an effort Plataea resisted by allying with Athens. After Boeotians fought on the Persian side in 479 BCE the league lapsed, and it was refounded after the defeat of Athens at Coronea in 447 BCE.
boeotian-league.r: The Hellenica Oxyrhynchia describes its 5th-century constitution: Boeotia was divided into eleven districts, each supplying a boeotarch, sixty federal councillors, soldiers and taxes in proportion, with Thebes holding four shares. Member cities kept local councils of propertied citizens. The federal coinage carried the Boeotian shield.
boeotian-league.e: The King's Peace dissolved it in 386 BCE, but Pelopidas and Epaminondas revived it after 379 BCE and defeated Sparta at Leuctra. Alexander destroyed Thebes in 335 BCE; a Hellenistic league continued until Rome dissolved it in 171 BCE.

barawa.t: A small Somali port city known for its Islamic scholarship and its own Bantu language, Chimiini, spoken by the Bravanese.
barawa.o: Barawa, or Brava, developed as a coastal trading town on the southern Somali coast in the early second millennium, settled by Somali Tunni clans together with Arab and Swahili-speaking merchants. Arab geographers mention it from around the 12th century, and its people developed the distinct Chimiini dialect of Swahili.
barawa.r: The town was governed by its leading families and religious notables rather than a strong monarchy. It traded hides, ivory and grain from the Shabelle and Jubba valleys, and was famous as a centre of Islamic learning, later linked with the Qadiriyya brotherhood. It resisted the Portuguese, who sacked it in 1506, and was for long tributary to the Ajuran Sultanate.
barawa.e: After Ajuran's decline Barawa came under Omani influence and in 1871 under the Sultanate of Zanzibar. Zanzibar leased the Benadir ports to Italy, and Barawa became part of Italian Somaliland. Its Bravanese community survives, though much reduced by the civil war after 1991.

banate-of-leitha.t: State proclaimed by Hungarian irregulars in 1921 to stop the transfer of Burgenland to Austria, whose resistance led to the plebiscite that kept Sopron Hungarian.
banate-of-leitha.o: The peace treaties of Saint-Germain and Trianon assigned German-speaking western Hungary, later called Burgenland, to Austria. When the handover began in August 1921, Hungarian irregulars of the Ragged Guard attacked Austrian gendarmes. On 4 October 1921 their commander, Pál Prónay, proclaimed the independent Banate of Leitha at Oberwart.
banate-of-leitha.r: The banate was a military occupation run by the irregulars, with a provisional administration and its own stamps; the Hungarian government officially disowned it while using it as a bargaining chip. Its population was mostly German-speaking, with Croatian and Hungarian minorities.
banate-of-leitha.e: Under Italian mediation the Venice Protocol of October 1921 agreed a plebiscite in Sopron, and the irregulars withdrew in November. Burgenland passed to Austria, while Sopron voted in December 1921 to stay in Hungary.

banovina-of-croatia.t: Autonomous Croatian province created in 1939 in a late attempt to settle the Serb-Croat conflict within the Kingdom of Yugoslavia.
banovina-of-croatia.o: The Kingdom of Yugoslavia had been divided in 1929 into banovinas that ignored historic borders. With war looming, the regent Prince Paul sought agreement with the Croatian Peasant Party, and the Cvetković-Maček Agreement of 26 August 1939 merged the Sava and Littoral banovinas with parts of Bosnia, Herzegovina, Srem and the Dubrovnik area into one Banovina of Croatia.
banovina-of-croatia.r: The banovina had autonomy over internal administration, education, justice and the economy under a ban, Ivan Šubašić, while Vladko Maček became deputy prime minister of Yugoslavia. A Croatian Sabor was planned but never elected. Serbs in the banovina feared Croatian domination, while the separatist Ustaše rejected any settlement within Yugoslavia.
banovina-of-croatia.e: After the Axis invasion of April 1941, the Ustaše proclaimed the Independent State of Croatia on 10 April, ending the banovina. Its borders influenced later debates about Croatia's territory, including the partition of Bosnia discussed in the 1990s.
banovina-of-croatia.re: Catholic and Orthodox Christianity, Sunni Islam

beylik-of-shahrisabz.t: A Kenagas Uzbek beylik around Shahrisabz that defied the emirs of Bukhara until Russia conquered it in 1870.
beylik-of-shahrisabz.o: Shahrisabz, the old city of Kesh and birthplace of Timur, was the stronghold of the Kenagas Uzbek tribe, which long resisted the Manghit Emirate of Bukhara. In the mid-19th century the Kenagas beks under Jura Beg and Baba Beg established effective independence.
beylik-of-shahrisabz.r: The beks ruled a fertile oasis on the Qashqadarya with the neighbouring town of Kitab, fortifying it against Bukhara. They exploited the emirate's conflicts with Russia and Kokand, at times accepting nominal Bukharan overlordship. Little is recorded of their internal government.
beylik-of-shahrisabz.e: In 1870 a Russian force under General Abramov stormed Shahrisabz and handed it to the Emirate of Bukhara, then a Russian protectorate. Jura Beg and Baba Beg fled to Kokand.

brigantes.t: The largest British confederation, ruling much of northern England under Queen Cartimandua until Rome conquered it after a civil war in the 70s.
brigantes.o: The Brigantes were a grouping of many communities across the Pennines and northern England, from the Mersey and Humber to the Tyne. Their name is linked to the goddess Brigantia. By the time of the Roman invasion of 43 they were under the rule of Queen Cartimandua, who made a treaty with Rome and governed as a client ruler.
brigantes.r: The confederation was loosely held, combining upland pastoralists and lowland farmers, and had no coinage of its own. Its political centre may have been at Stanwick in North Yorkshire, where vast earthwork enclosures were built in the 1st century. Cartimandua handed the fugitive Caratacus to the Romans in 51, and later her divorce from her consort Venutius split the Brigantes into rival factions.
brigantes.e: In 69 Venutius drove Cartimandua out, and Roman troops could only rescue her. Petillius Cerialis then conquered the Brigantes from 71, with the legion based at York. The southern territory became a civitas centred on Isurium Brigantum, Aldborough, in Roman Britain.

bastuli.t: A mixed Iberian and Phoenician people of the coast between Gibraltar and Almería, known to Greek writers as the Blastophoenicians.
bastuli.o: The Bastuli lived along the southern coast of Iberia, roughly from the Strait of Gibraltar to Almería, from the mid-first millennium BCE. Ancient writers called them Bastuli-Poeni or Blastophoenicians, reflecting a population mixing native people with Phoenician and Punic settlers of towns such as Malaka, Sexi and Abdera.
bastuli.r: They lived from farming, fishing and fish salting, and their region minted coins in a distinctive Libyphoenician script. Little is known about their government, and it is debated whether they formed a people at all or were a label for the coastal Punicised communities.
bastuli.e: After the Roman conquest of the south in 206 BCE they came under Hispania Ulterior and took part in the revolt of 197 BCE. Later they were absorbed into Baetica.

bahurutshe-chiefdom.t: The senior house of the Tswana, whose stone-walled capital Kaditshwene impressed early 19th-century visitors as one of the largest towns in southern Africa.
bahurutshe-chiefdom.o: The Bahurutshe trace their descent from the founding Tswana lineage, from which the Bakwena and other groups later branched. By the 16th century they were settled in the Marico district of the western highveld, where they built aggregated towns with stone-walled cattle enclosures.
bahurutshe-chiefdom.r: Chiefs ruled large towns divided into wards, each under a headman, with public assemblies (kgotla) for justice and debate. The economy combined cattle herding, cereal farming and skilled metalworking in iron and copper. When the missionary John Campbell visited Kaditshwene in 1820 he estimated its population at 16,000 and admired its metal crafts and trade.
bahurutshe-chiefdom.e: Kaditshwene was destroyed in the wars of the early 1820s, and the Hurutshe later suffered under Mzilikazi's Ndebele. Reassembled under Moilwa in the Marico valley, they came under the rule of the Transvaal Boer republic after 1852, though Hurutshe communities persist around Zeerust and in Botswana.

bangwato-kingdom.t: The largest Tswana chiefdom, ruled from Shoshong and later Palapye, whose king Khama III helped keep Botswana out of Company rule.
bangwato-kingdom.o: The Bangwato branched off from the Bakwena in the 18th century and settled in what is now central Botswana. After the disruptions of the 1820s they grew under Sekgoma I, with Shoshong as their capital, absorbing many refugees and subject groups.
bangwato-kingdom.r: Chiefs ruled through the kgotla and ward headmen, with cattle as the basis of wealth. Shoshong became a key stop on the missionary and trade road to the north. Khama III, a Christian, became chief in 1875, banned alcohol trading, moved the capital to Palapye in 1889 and promoted the London Missionary Society church.
bangwato-kingdom.e: The Bangwato joined the Bechuanaland Protectorate in 1885. In 1895 Khama travelled to London with other chiefs to resist transfer to the British South Africa Company. His grandson Seretse Khama became Botswana's first president in 1966.

banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya.t: The last Almoravid family, which crossed from Majorca to wage a fifty-year war against the Almohads across Ifriqiya and the central Maghreb.
banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya.o: The Banu Ghaniya, descendants of an Almoravid princess, held the Balearic Islands as Banu Ghaniya Majorca after the fall of the Almoravid Empire. In 1184 Ali ibn Ghaniya landed at Bejaia, seized the city from the Almohad Caliphate and opened a war to restore Almoravid rule, recognising the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad.
banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya.r: There was no fixed capital. The Banu Ghaniya fought as a roaming power, allied with Arab tribes such as the Banu Sulaym and, for a time, with Qaraqush. Under Ali's brother Yahya ibn Ghaniya they took Tunis and Mahdia around 1203, devastating towns and countryside across Ifriqiya and Tripolitania.
banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya.e: The Almohad caliph al-Nasir retook Mahdia and Tunis in 1205 to 1206 and installed a Hafsid governor, whose successors kept up the fight. Yahya was driven into the desert and died in the 1230s, ending the movement. The chaos helped the Hafsid Sultanate emerge.

bastarnae.t: Probably Germanic people of the lower Danube and Carpathians who fought for Macedon against Rome and later joined the Goths.
bastarnae.o: The Bastarnae appeared north of the lower Danube around 200 BCE, the first Germanic-speaking people known to Greek and Roman writers, though some ancient authors thought them Celts. One branch, the Peucini, lived on the island of Peuce in the Danube delta.
bastarnae.r: They were a warlike confederation of tribes, valued as mercenaries. Philip V and Perseus of Macedon recruited them against Rome, and the Zarubintsy and Poienești-Lukashevka archaeological cultures are often linked to them. In 62 BCE they defeated Gaius Antonius Hybrida near Histria. In 29 BCE Marcus Licinius Crassus defeated them and killed their king Deldo in single combat.
bastarnae.e: Under the empire they remained a frontier people, joining the Goths and Carpi in 3rd-century raids. Around 280 the emperor Probus settled a large number of Bastarnae in Thrace, after which they disappear as a distinct people.

belarusian-peoples-republic.t: The first Belarusian attempt at independence, proclaimed under German occupation in 1918, whose Rada still survives in exile.
belarusian-peoples-republic.o: After the Russian Revolution Belarusian activists formed a Rada in Minsk. While German troops occupied the city, the Rada issued a series of charters, and on 25 March 1918 the Third Constituent Charter declared the Belarusian People's Republic independent of Russia. Jan Sierada became the first chairman of the Rada.
belarusian-peoples-republic.r: The republic never controlled much territory or had an army, as real power lay with the German military. Its government, led by figures such as Raman Skirmunt and later Anton Lutskevich, organised schools in the Belarusian language and sought recognition abroad. It issued passports and sent missions to neighbouring states.
belarusian-peoples-republic.e: When the Germans withdrew in December 1918 the Bolsheviks took Minsk and set up the Socialist Soviet Republic of Byelorussia. The Rada went into exile, where it has continued under successive leaders, making it the world's oldest government in exile. 25 March is marked by Belarusian opposition as Freedom Day.

black-sea-cossack-host.t: A Cossack army formed from former Zaporozhians, which settled the Kuban frontier and founded the city now called Krasnodar.
black-sea-cossack-host.o: In 1787, on the eve of war with the Ottoman Empire, Prince Grigory Potemkin gathered former Zaporozhian Cossacks into the Host of Loyal Zaporozhians. Led by Sydir Bilyi, Zakhary Chepiha and Anton Holovaty, they fought at Ochakiv and Izmail, and in 1790 they were renamed the Black Sea Cossack Host.
black-sea-cossack-host.r: In 1792 Catherine II granted the Host the lands of the Taman peninsula and the right bank of the Kuban, and in 1793 they founded Yekaterinodar as their capital. The Cossacks kept elected officers and a Zaporozhian tradition, farming and guarding a fortified line against the Circassians across the Kuban.
black-sea-cossack-host.e: The Host fought throughout the Caucasian War. In 1860 it was merged with part of the Caucasus Line Cossack Host to form the Kuban Cossack Host. Its Ukrainian heritage shaped the speech and culture of the Kuban region.

byblos.t: Byblos, an ancient Phoenician port on the Lebanese coast that shipped cedar to Egypt for over two thousand years and gave the Greeks their word for papyrus.
byblos.o: Gubla, as its people called it, is among the oldest continuously inhabited towns in the world. By c. 2600 BCE it had become a walled city whose harbour supplied cedar and resin from the Lebanon mountains to the pharaohs of the Old Kingdom of Egypt, receiving gold, linen and papyrus in return.
byblos.r: Kings ruled under the protection of the city's goddess, the Baalat Gebal, whose temple received Egyptian offerings. In the 14th century BCE its king Rib-Hadda sent dozens of the Amarna letters begging Egypt for help. The sarcophagus of King Ahiram bears one of the earliest inscriptions in the Phoenician alphabet, which Byblos helped to shape.
byblos.e: Byblos lost commercial leadership to Tyre and Sidon in the Iron Age and paid tribute to the Assyrian Empire, the Chaldean Empire and the Achaemenid Empire in turn. It submitted peacefully to Alexander of the Macedonian Empire in 332 BCE, ending its independent kingship. The town of Jbeil still occupies the site.
